lesson.title: Homozygous and Heterozygous: Matching Alleles or Mixed Alleles
lesson.summary: An organism is homozygous for a gene if its two alleles are identical, either both dominant or both recessive, and heterozygous if the two alleles differ, and this distinction determines both what gametes it can produce and whether its genotype is hidden by its phenotype.
lesson.body:
An organism is homozygous for a gene if the two alleles it carries at that locus are identical to each other. This can mean homozygous dominant, such as PP, or homozygous recessive, such as pp. An organism is heterozygous if the two alleles it carries are different from each other, such as Pp. This vocabulary is really just a more precise way of describing the genotypes introduced in the previous chapter, since every genotype for a single gene is either homozygous or heterozygous.

This distinction matters for two practical reasons. First, it determines what gametes an individual can produce. Because the law of segregation simply separates whatever two alleles an individual carries into different gametes, a homozygous individual, PP or pp, can only produce one type of gamete for that gene, since both alleles being separated are identical, all its gametes carry P, or all carry p. A heterozygous individual, Pp, produces two types of gametes in equal proportion, half carrying P and half carrying p, exactly as used in the worked crosses in earlier chapters. Second, it determines whether an organism's genotype can be inferred just by looking at its phenotype. Because of dominance, a homozygous dominant individual, PP, and a heterozygous individual, Pp, look identical, both purple, so phenotype alone cannot distinguish them. Only a homozygous recessive individual, pp, has a phenotype that directly and unambiguously reveals its genotype.

The Pp by Pp cross makes this concrete once more. Among the offspring, 1 out of 4 are homozygous dominant, PP, 2 out of 4 are heterozygous, Pp, and 1 out of 4 are homozygous recessive, pp, a genotype ratio of 1 to 2 to 1. Phenotypically, 3 out of 4 are purple, combining the PP and Pp individuals, and 1 out of 4 is white. This same distinction underlies a classic genetics technique called a test cross. If a purple-flowered plant's genotype is unknown, it could be either PP or Pp, breeding it with a known homozygous recessive plant, pp, helps reveal which. If all the offspring turn out purple, the unknown parent was most likely PP, since a Pp parent would be expected to also produce some white offspring. If roughly half the offspring turn out white, the unknown parent was heterozygous, Pp.

Every cross worked through in this unit so far, a single heterozygous individual bred with another single heterozygous individual for one gene, is itself an example of a broader, formally named technique. That technique, the monohybrid cross, is the subject of the final chapter in this sequence.
